data.reasoning: The package is safe. The PKGBUILD uses standard AUR patterns: sources are pinned to a specific upstream git tag (2.3.0) with SHA-256 checksums, the prepare() function performs a git cherry-pick of a hard-coded commit from the same repository to backport a stack-smashing fix (normal practice, no network fetch of untrusted content), and build/package functions use standard CMake invocations. The .SRCINFO correctly reflects the PKGBUILD metadata. The .nvchecker.toml is a standard version-tracking config pointing to the legitimate upstream GitHub repository. No code injection, no execution of fetched content, no fetching from unrelated hosts.
data.disagreement_analysis: The disagreement is purely a tool error, not a substantive security disagreement. Report 1 (qwen3-235b) failed to audit .SRCINFO due to an HTTP 400 API error, resulting in an inconclusive overall verdict. Report 2 (deepseek-v4-flash) successfully reviewed all three files and found them safe. Both models agreed on the PKGBUILD and .nvchecker.toml assessments. The inconclusive result in Report 1 does not reflect any security concern—it is a coverage gap from a transient API failure.
coverage_issues: Report 1 (qwen3-235b) failed to review .SRCINFO due to LLM API error (HTTP 400 BadRequestError), leaving that file inconclusive
learnings: When one report has a tool error causing inconclusive status on a non-critical metadata file (.SRCINFO) and another report successfully reviews all files with a clean verdict, the successful report should be weighted appropriately rather than treating the situation as a genuine security disagreement.

The audit tool should distinguish between 'inconclusive due to tool error' and 'inconclusive due to genuine uncertainty' in its escalation logic—tool errors on metadata files should not trigger full re-audits when another model has already covered those files successfully.
